item.title: Clancy Hearing Focuses on Holdout Juror
item.description:
A hearing Monday in the case of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman charged with murdering her three children, was dominated by the question of whether the lone juror who wanted to convict her should have been disqualified from serving.

Kevin Reddington, a lawyer for Ms. Clancy, suggested during the hearing that the holdout juror, Michael Desronvil, had been dishonest during jury selection by failing to tell the court that he had been arrested on domestic violence charges in 2021 that were later dismissed. But Heather O’Connor, a lawyer for Mr. Desronvil, said that he had checked a box on his juror questionnaire to indicate past involvement with the legal system.

Ms. Clancy’s lawyers “could have followed up on” his disclosure during jury selection, Ms. O’Connor said, “but they didn’t.” She repeatedly defended her client’s conduct, at one point saying that “we are here” because her client “did not vote the way the defense needed.”

Prosecutors did not reveal on Monday whether they intended to retry Ms. Clancy on first-degree murder charges or reduce the charges, which would allow for a bench trial before a judge instead of a jury.

The hearing’s focus on Mr. Desronvil, and his role in the mistrial that upended the case against Ms. Clancy in September, stemmed from a defense motion asking for further investigation of his conduct. The defense is also seeking dismissal of the murder charges against Ms. Clancy on double jeopardy grounds, asserting that the mistrial could have been avoided if the judge had dug deeper into a claim by other jurors that the holdout was not following the law.

Specifically, other members of the jury complained in notes sent to the judge during deliberations that Mr. Desronvil was ignoring the rules regarding reasonable doubt. While the judge questioned all 12 jurors about it, he rejected a defense request to replace the holdout with an alternate. Soon after, he declared a mistrial.

Mr. Desronvil released a statement in late September saying he had no doubt that Ms. Clancy was guilty.

Judge Sullivan did not rule on either request by the defense during the tense hearing, nor did he set a tentative new trial date. Instead, he scheduled another hearing for Nov. 16.

Martin Weinberg, another of Ms. Clancy’s lawyers, said at the hearing that the jurors’ notes “cried out” for more investigation, and that the judge’s failure to dig deeper had jeopardized Ms. Clancy’s right to a trial with 12 unbiased jurors.

Mr. Reddington also cited other jurors’ claims in interviews after the mistrial that Mr. Desronvil had used his cellphone during deliberations. Mr. Reddington said the court should try to determine if the juror had done research related to the trial, which could have been grounds for his dismissal.

In response, prosecutors said that any such inquiry should not be limited to a single juror. “If the door is open to examining this juror, it would be open on all jurors,” said Jennifer Sprague, an assistant district attorney for Plymouth County.

Ms. Clancy’s case attracted an enormous national audience during her six-week trial. Public reaction to the outcome was fiercely divided, with the juror who voted to convict Ms. Clancy at the center of the debate.

After the hearing on Monday, Ms. O’Connor, Mr. Desronvil’s lawyer, said her client had been questioned by prosecutors about his recent criminal history during the jury selection process last summer, an inquiry prompted by his answers on the juror questionnaire. After he told prosecutors that he did not harbor lingering ill will toward their office or the court system as a result of his experience, Ms. O’Connor said, neither the prosecutors nor Ms. Clancy’s lawyers moved to strike him from consideration for the jury.

Past criminal charges do not automatically disqualify prospective jurors. Under Massachusetts law, only people who have been convicted of a felony in the last seven years are ineligible to serve.

Ms. Clancy, 36, has remained in custody at a state hospital since the mistrial. She appeared to pay close attention to the arguments at Monday’s hearing.

Pressed by the judge on Monday about how they plan to proceed with the case, prosecutors declined to say. “We’re not at that point yet,” Ms. Sprague said.

Timothy Cruz, the Plymouth County district attorney, has built a reputation as hard-nosed and uncompromising. But his decision about whether to reduce the charges may be influenced by the jury’s near-consensus in the summer trial, when 11 of 12 jurors concluded that Ms. Clancy should be found not guilty by reason of insanity.

If found guilty of first-degree murder, Ms. Clancy would face a sentence of life in prison; the sentence for second-degree murder includes the possibility of parole after 15 years.

Ms. Clancy’s lawyer argued at trial that she was not criminally responsible for killing Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, in 2023 because she was in the throes of severe postpartum mental illness at the time. After strangling the children, Ms. Clancy cut her wrists and throat and jumped from a window, sustaining spinal injuries that left her paralyzed.

The trial revived a national debate about postpartum mental illness, its treatment and how criminal cases involving postpartum women should be treated by the courts. The defense focused on Ms. Clancy’s persistent but unsuccessful efforts to find effective mental health care in the months and weeks before the killings, as she descended into anxiety and depression and struggled with intrusive thoughts about harming her children.

The online furor around the case has raised concerns about the prospect of seating another jury for a second trial, given the trepidation many prospective jurors might feel about their possible exposure to criticism and threats.

item.title: A 20-Year-Old Was One Pilot of the Jet That Plunged to Earth in Florida
item.description:
One of the pilots of a private jet that plummeted to the ground on Sunday afternoon in Florida, killing all nine people on board, was a 20-year-old aviator named Nathalia Filgueiras, her mother said on Monday.

Ms. Filgueiras, of Boca Raton, Fla., had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time and received her pilot’s license at 17, according to her mother, Camila Corteleti. She said her daughter had worked for Upper Jets, a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale, and was co-pilot of Sunday’s flight.

The other pilot on the jet has not been identified, and it’s not known who was at the controls when the plane began to fall.

Ms. Corteleti said her daughter had been passionate about flying since childhood, a love forged soaring the skies with her father, who is a recreational pilot. She recalled that her daughter, as a child, used to enjoy going to the Boca Raton Airport to watch planes taking off and landing, and she announced when she was about 12 that she wanted to be a pilot.

“She loved the freedom,” Ms. Corteleti said. “It was completely different seeing the world from the top.”

Efforts to reach Upper Jets were not immediately successful.

The company’s plane, a Learjet 60, which had been traveling from Texas to the Bahamas, crashed down in a residential area of Palm Beach County, Fla., leaving a smoldering crater and wreckage in the street. Investigators were working on Monday to determine what happened.

In 2023, CBS12, a news outlet based in South Florida, reported that Ms. Filgueiras had gotten her private pilot’s license when she was a senior in high school. “I like being different than everyone,” she said in a video interview at the time.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement on Sunday that all of the people on the plane had died. There was no information available about the identities of the passengers. Officials said that it did not appear that any people on the ground had been injured.

In the moments before the plane crashed, a pilot radioed air traffic controllers, and she said that the plane was facing some rain, and “light, clear ice that is manageable, and moderate turbulence,” according to archived communications with air traffic controllers in Miami on Sunday afternoon.

The woman asked if she could climb to 37,000 feet, but soon after she desperately declared mayday, a life-threatening emergency, to air traffic controllers. She screamed that the plane was descending at a rate of 20,000 feet per minute. “We’re going to crash into the ground,” she said.

Jared Isaacman, the administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, said in a social media post on Monday that it was too early to speculate on what might have gone wrong, pointing to a range of possible factors including structural problems, maintenance history and weather.

He added that the airline charter industry often hires early career pilots so that they can gain experience before moving on to work for commercial airlines. Co-pilots, he said, are empowered to communicate about flight problems.

“She was doing her job,” Mr. Isaacman said of Ms. Filgueiras, “communicating with A.T.C. right to the end in a terrifying situation. She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die.”

item.title: Backlash to Immigration Crackdown Creates a Challenge for Republicans
item.description:
President Trump returned to the White House calling for “mass deportations now,” after anger over illegal immigration drove his voters to the polls in 2024. But two years later, amid high-profile raids and deadly ICE shootings, immigration politics have been scrambled once again, creating unpredictable fault lines in the hours leading up to Election Day.

Public polling suggests that voters are now more likely to trust Democrats on immigration policy, although Republican voters remain more motivated by the issue. And while some Latino voting-rights activists worry that recent immigration raids in California and elsewhere could suppress Hispanic turnout, others are optimistic that the opposite is true in some of the most competitive congressional districts in the country.

“Republicans are really out of step with where Americans are with immigration, just like how Democrats were out of step in 2024,” said Senator Ruben Gallego, a Democrat who won in Arizona two years ago while calling for stricter immigration enforcement. “They wanted the chaos to be done, but what is happening now is not what they wanted. They are not for heavy-handed immigration forces. They are not for racial profiling; they see the sob stories.”

In the first two years of his second term, Mr. Trump has moved aggressively to overhaul the nation’s immigration system, and the southern border has largely been shut down. Attempted illegal border crossings have plummeted from a peak of nearly 250,000 in November 2023 to about 11,000 this past August.

But the administration also unleashed an enormous enforcement apparatus that has drawn widespread criticism. Large-scale raids have unfolded in Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis. Federal detention capacity has more than doubled through a network of local jail contracts, retrofitted warehouses and tent cities.

And the administration has all but dismantled pathways to asylum, reduced refugee admissions to a trickle and stripped temporary deportation protections from roughly one million migrants who entered the country during the Biden administration. At the same time, the government has pressured immigrants into self-deportation and pushed immigration judges to expedite dockets, keeping more people behind bars and deporting hundreds to countries where they have no personal ties.

At campaign events, the president has compared his record favorably to that of his predecessor. At a recent rally in Iowa, he blamed Democrats for the flood of migrants entering the country during the Biden administration and warned that it would happen again if Republicans lost the election. “It was an invasion — it was like a military invasion,” he said. “They will do it again. They’re going to open up the border.”

But his assertive approach has created a backlash among voters.

Voters in 2024 were more likely to list immigration as a top issue than in this midterm year, when economic concerns are driving the conversation even more. And immigration continues to be more of a motivating issue for Republicans than Democrats. But opposition to the Trump administration’s policies has changed the calculus significantly. In the most recent New York Times/Siena poll, half of all voters said they trusted Democrats on the issue, while 46 percent said they trusted Republicans. That is a striking reversal from just two years ago, when Mr. Trump held an 11-point advantage on immigration in the Times/Siena national poll.

Immigration has helped drive the gains that Democrats appear to be making with Hispanic voters throughout the country. While Latino voters were divided on which party to trust on immigration in 2024, they now give Democrats a 27-point lead. And about one in five Latinos said immigration was the most important issue to their vote, according to the Times/Siena poll, compared to just 6 percent in September.

The Rev. Samuel Rodriguez, who leads the National Hispanic Christian Leadership Conference, which includes thousands of churches, said Republicans had squandered a unique opportunity to make politically popular changes to immigration policies.

“They could have developed a viable solution to immigration and bring a secure border, and get rid of egregious criminals,” he said. “Instead, you’re picking up people who have been making their lives for years, and even ministers. What are we doing here? What just happened?”

The issue could help Democrats in dozens of tight races throughout the country, particularly in California, Colorado, Florida and Texas, where immigrant-heavy communities have felt the impact of the crackdown. In September, Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican, released a television ad warning Mr. Trump that his aggressive tactics had “gone too far” and left many of his Hispanic supporters feeling “betrayed.” Like many Republicans who represent areas with a large Latino population, Ms. Salazar is in a surprisingly tight re-election campaign in a district where Mr. Trump won with a double-digit lead.

One such district sits in the heart of California’s Central Valley, where Representative David Valadao, a Republican, has repeatedly faced serious challengers since he was first elected in 2012. The district stretches across the state’s agricultural heartland. Roughly 65 percent of registered voters are Latino, and Democrats have long outnumbered Republicans.

Recent immigration raids in Mr. Valadao’s district have gripped some farmworker communities with so much fear that local markets began delivering groceries to immigrant families afraid to leave home. Local residents say the rise in traffic stops and other arrests has kept Latino workers from reporting to work and emptied Latino businesses.

Mr. Valadao has long said he would support a legal pathway for undocumented residents who have been in the country for many years and have not committed crimes. He has also urged the administration to prioritize deporting violent criminals rather than agricultural workers.

In the final days of the campaign, Mr. Valadao’s Democratic challenger, Randy Villegas, 31, a college professor and the son of Mexican immigrants, has seized on the issue of immigration, attacking Mr. Valadao for supporting legislation that tripled the budget for federal immigration enforcement. He blames Mr. Valadao for enabling a deportation campaign he says is harming agricultural workers and the economy.

“It’s shameful, it is despicable and we deserve a member of Congress who has a spine to actually stand up for our immigrant communities,” Mr. Villegas said in an interview.

In a statement, Mr. Valadao said that he has worked with both parties to “fix our broken immigration system” and that “meaningful immigration will require bipartisan cooperation.”

“I understand the concerns about enforcement activities, but based on my conversations with the administration and producers around my district, there’s no evidence that farmworkers are being targeted,” he added.

Immigration continues to be a campaign issue for Republican candidates for Congress, but Democrats in this election have increasingly used it as a line of attack, too, including in political advertising.

Democrats have produced about 320 ads focused on immigration — more than five times the number in the 2022 midterms, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm. Republicans have created about 890, a slight uptick from four years ago.

Across competitive races in the Southwest, Andrea Flores, a lawyer and immigration policy adviser in the Obama and Biden administrations, said she had seen a slate of Democratic candidates more willing to “flip the script” by tying immigration policy to labor shortages and the battered economy.

In New Mexico, Representative Gabe Vasquez, a Democrat locked in a tight bid for a third term, has championed visas for child care providers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who has pulled within striking distance of unseating Gov. Greg Abbott, addressed reporters from an uncompleted construction site, where she said immigrant workers did not feel safe showing up.

Still, Ms. Flores said Democrats have largely focused on attacking Republicans, rather than articulating their own policy agenda. “There is an urgent need to define what they are for on the issue because just being against ICE is not enough,” she said.

In the run-up to the election, some voting rights advocates have worried about the impact of immigration enforcement on turnout.

Although voters are by definition U.S. citizens, many fear being harassed or even detained by immigration agents, said Cesar Fierros, a spokesman for a group called Living United for Change in Arizona.

“There was a time when there was a belief that, ‘Hey, I am a citizen. I am not undocumented. I don’t have to worry about it,’” he said. “But now you are seeing U.S. citizens arrested and detained.”

But so far, early data suggests an increase in early voting turnout among Latinos, including in Texas and California.

“If this was meant as voter intimidation, it’s not working,” said Andrea Guerrero, executive director at Alliance San Diego, a legal services and voter mobilization organization. “Voting is surging in San Diego County and in California.”

Ruth Igielnik and Miriam Jordan contributed reporting.

item.title: Judge Throws Out Charges Against Former F.B.I. Officials
item.description:
A federal magistrate judge on Monday threw out charges against two former F.B.I. intelligence officials accused of lying to Congress, excoriating prosecutors for what he described as a failure of one of their most basic responsibilities: showing there was any probable cause that crimes had been committed in the first place.

In an emotional, hourlong address from the bench in Federal District Court in Washington, the magistrate judge, Zia M. Faruqui, said that the case against the former officials — Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides — was a rushed, political prosecution ordered by the White House intended to affect the upcoming midterm elections. Two weeks ago, the administration charged the former officials with falsely minimizing their work on investigations involving Hunter Biden, the son of the former president.

Judge Faruqui blasted the U.S. attorney’s office in Washington for how it handled the case, admonishing prosecutors for trying to avoid some of the fundamental checks and balances of the criminal justice system. At the same time, he apologized directly to Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides for having been “dragged through this process” of being charged by the same federal government they had served for decades.

“I am deeply troubled by what happened here in this case,” Judge Faruqui said. “What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization.”

The dismissal of the charges was the Justice Department’s latest failure to follow through on President Trump’s relentless demands to take revenge against a long list of people who have run afoul of him. In recent months, both judges and grand juries have repeatedly rejected the department’s attempts to prosecute the president’s enemies in a growing — and humiliating — series of legal defeats.

Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides drew the president’s ire because of their work on the F.B.I.’s Foreign Influence Task Force, a group created after Russia interfered in the 2016 election. The task force was designed to help intelligence agencies monitor clandestine efforts by foreign governments to manipulate American politics and in the weeks before the 2020 election it raised concerns that reports about Hunter Biden — especially those concerning a laptop that he left behind at a computer repair shop — may have been influenced by a Russian disinformation campaign.

From the outset, the case against them was a particularly bitter one, embodying a battle that has raged for nearly two years between the F.B.I.’s current leadership and the scores of agents who have been purged from the bureau because of their supposed disloyalty to Mr. Trump.

That rancor was on full display in court on Monday as several former F.B.I. agents — some fired by the bureau’s director, Kash Patel — showed up to cheer the dismissal of the case. Among those in the gallery were Brian Driscoll, the former acting director of the F.B.I.; Dave Sundberg, the former agent in charge of the bureau’s Washington field office; and Steven Jensen, another longtime F.B.I. leader.

Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides were charged in a complaint last month with making false statements during testimony they gave in 2023 to the House Judiciary Committee about the roles they had played in the bureau’s contentious investigations of the younger Mr. Biden and his laptop. But during his speech, Judge Faruqui dismantled almost every aspect of the government’s case. He pointed out that most of the false statements the two defendants were charged with making were not actually false, that none of the false statements were made knowingly and that none of them had any material effect on the congressional investigation which they were called upon to assist.

“That is not probable cause,” he said over and over.

Ms. Floris’s legal team hailed the dismissal of the case in a statement on Monday.

“The charges brought under the clearly discredited authority of the Department of Justice should never have been brought in the first place,” the statement said. “And while Nikki should never have had to endure this disgraceful public attack, we hope the courts continue to be a refuge for all citizens unlawfully targeted by the Trump administration.”

Judge Faruqui was allowed to weigh in on the viability of the case because prosecutors chose to charge Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides through a criminal complaint, not an indictment. Complaints require a judge to make a finding of probable cause whereas indictments require only a majority vote by a panel of grand jurors and do not require a judge’s approval.

But federal prosecutors in Washington have failed so often over the past two years to secure indictments from grand juries that they have grown wary of the panels — especially in politicized cases involving Mr. Trump’s opponents. While their complaint against Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides is dead, prosecutors could try to resuscitate the charges by asking a grand jury to approve them.

Judge Faruqui, who once worked as a prosecutor in the office that brought the charges, said it was clear to him that his former colleagues were worried about taking this case in particular to the grand jury given how often they had failed to obtain indictments.

“It is self-evident that the U.S. attorney’s office is avoiding taking this case to the grand jury,” he said, “and that is understandable given their poor record there lately, but it is also unbelievable.”

The judge left almost no part of the government’s efforts to prosecute Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides unscathed. He pointed to its politicized origins, saying that Mr. Patel had personally assigned the inquiry to the F.B.I.’s Kansas City field office one day after Mr. Trump, during a prime-time address, criticized bureau intelligence officials for supposedly suppressing evidence that China had interfered in the 2020 election.

Mr. Patel went so far as to specify the charges — conspiracy and obstruction — he wanted the agents in Kansas City to investigate. But when the agents failed to find any evidence to support those allegations, they quickly pivoted to examining the congressional testimony Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides had given the House committee and comparing it to hundreds of thousands of internal F.B.I. communications looking for discrepancies.

Judge Faruqui noted that one of the agents assigned to the case had testified last week that the investigation was widely viewed inside the Kansas City office as a “witch hunt.” The judge also said that the case had been conducted so hurriedly that the original complaint was riddled with factual errors.

The judge expressed incredulity that an investigation personally ordered by the president and directly overseen by the F.B.I.’s director — who often checked in with the case agents by video conference — could have been handled in such a slipshod manner.

“It’s preposterous,” he said, “but not illogical given the timeline.”

That timeline was directly connected to the midterm elections, Judge Faruqui said, adding that he could find no other reason the charges were brought in a rush last month other than to make a splash before voters went to the polls.

“There was simply no other event on the calendar except one — the midterms,” he said. “I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend that I cannot read a calendar.”

In a moment of levity, Judge Faruqui said he would never have expected to still be discussing Hunter Biden and his laptop in late 2026, adding that the subject was clearly an obsession for Mr. Trump and his congressional allies.

But he concluded his address on a somber note, asserting that the case had badly damaged the reputation of the F.B.I., greatly chilled Congress’s ability to get honest testimony from witnesses and further eroded confidence in the Justice Department.

He then apologized to Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides.

“I am sorry you have been dragged through this process,” he said. “I am sorry everyone has dragged through this process. But this is where we are.”

item.title: Accused of Voter Fraud, They Ended Up in Shackles
item.description:
It was before dawn when Amandeep Kaur turned herself in to federal authorities in downtown Los Angeles last Monday. Wrapped in a tasseled shawl, she paced and shivered as she waited outside the courthouse.

At 6:30 a.m., two plainclothes agents rounded the corner, served Ms. Kaur her arrest warrant and walked her to an unmarked vehicle, where they lightly searched her. She would be fingerprinted and taken into custody before appearing in front of a judge that afternoon.

Ms. Kaur, a 30-year-old from India, lives with her two young children, her husband and her in-laws in Rancho Palos Verdes, Calif. She speaks little English and is a legal permanent resident of the United States.

The government says in court documents that Ms. Kaur registered to vote in 2022, voted in the 2024 election — unlawfully, they say, because she is not a U.S. citizen — and then made false statements about that history on her naturalization application.

As of Friday, she was among more than 220 people across 28 states charged in connection with voting violations during President Trump’s second term — part of the administration’s far-reaching, monthslong effort to find, arrest and publicize instances of voter fraud.

In the process, people like Ms. Kaur have been caught up in a disorienting and often demeaning experience: Taken by federal agents from their homes, or ordered to turn themselves in. Portrayed as criminals by the country many of them are trying to become citizens of, with their names and faces circulating online. Forced to appear before judges, in some cases in shackles. Some people have been kept in custody for days. At least one man remains in a Texas jail.

Election officials in California and other states have condemned the government’s crackdown, saying its system for identifying suspected violators is severely flawed, based on incomplete information, and has been rife with mistakes, including targeting people who are citizens.

The backdrop to the latest round of charges is the fierce midterm battle in which Democrats are in position to retake the House and possibly the Senate. Mr. Trump has repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that Democrats have stolen past elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally. He has called for national measures to prevent fraud that include voter identification, proof of citizenship and restrictions on mail balloting.

State audits and studies have repeatedly found that noncitizen voting is extremely rare, and there have been no instances in which their votes are known to have swayed an election.

The New York Times spent more than a week contacting people whom the administration charged in connection with violating election law. In interviews, some of the defendants and their family members cited language barriers, confusion about the voting process and unexpectedly receiving ballots in the mail as reasons for mistakenly registering or casting a vote.

Others denied the allegations completely. They said they were shocked when the authorities contacted them or showed up at their doors.

The Homeland Security Department did not respond to a request for comment. Nor did the Justice Department. It has described the arrests as part of a coordinated effort “to combat and root out fraud in U.S. elections and protect electoral integrity.”

Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general, has said that “every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen.”

Ms. Kaur’s husband, Kulwinder Ghotra, said that his wife, who speaks Punjabi, began receiving voter information in the mail after taking a driving test at the Department of Motor Vehicles. Believing she was eligible, he said, she voted in 2024.

“She was confused,” said Mr. Ghotra, 38. “She said there was no translation there at the voting center.”

Ms. Kaur was eventually charged with making false statements on her naturalization application — a felony that carries a maximum sentence of up to five years in federal prison, a fine, or both, and which can result in deportation. She declined to be interviewed about her case while it is pending.

Mr. Ghotra now fears that his wife could be deported. The couple has two children, ages 3 and 5.

Last week, a judge ruled that Ms. Kaur could return home in advance of her hearing this month. A translator relayed this to Ms. Kaur in Punjabi.

She was escorted from the courtroom in shackles and handcuffs.

Early on Oct. 19, federal agents banged on the door of Omar Alexander Muñoz, a 72-year-old from Belize, at his home in Commerce, Calif. They threatened to break down the door, Mr. Muñoz said in an interview.

He said the agents pulled his arms behind his back to handcuff him, injuring his shoulder and his neck, both of which he said he had recently had surgery on.

Several police cars, as well as members of the media, were stationed outside his home during the arrest, Mr. Muñoz said.

“They were positioned in a way, waiting,” he said of the reporters. “I was used to make a show of voter fraud.”

The Justice Department, the did not respond to questions about whether or not agents had notified the news media in advance of the arrest, or whether they had used excessive force.

Voting rights experts have called arrests of individuals like Mr. Muñoz performative stunts intended to bolster the government’s legal effort to disqualify California voters.

“This is to serve a political purpose, and that political purpose is to support the civil suit, as well as to support Donald Trump’s claims of a big problem of noncitizen voters,” said Richard Hasen, a law professor and election law expert at the University of California, Los Angeles.

“My first reaction was: These are the best cases they have?” Mr. Hasen said. “Like this guy, Omar Muñoz, like, he’s the perp? Please.”

A legal permanent resident of the United States for more than five decades, Mr. Munoz was charged with illegally registering to vote and making false statements on his citizenship application.

He maintains his innocence. In an interview with CBS News, he said he believed someone else may have used his name.

Though President Trump has made a particular example of California, charges of voter fraud have been made across more than two dozen states, including Florida, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and Texas.

Khalwinder Singh Bhengura, of Arlington, Texas, is originally from India and became a permanent legal resident in 2022.

Mr. Bhengura, 70, who speaks Punjabi, had been living in Texas with his wife, according to his brother-in-law Jay Chima. But he had an old habit of nodding along to things he did not understand in order to seem agreeable, Mr. Chima said, and “his English skills are nil.”

In September, Mr. Bhengura was charged with making false statements while registering to vote, and with casting a ballot unlawfully in 2024. He took his case to trial and pleaded not guilty; his lawyers argued that there was not enough evidence to prove that he had voted. They also worried about his ability to comprehend a fast-moving trial.

On Tuesday, a jury found Mr. Bhengura guilty of making false statements of citizenship in order to register to vote, and of voting by an alien in a federal election.

After the verdict was read, Mr. Bhengura was jailed. He remains in custody.

Nicole Knox, a lawyer for Mr. Bhengura, said she found the jailing appalling, and that she worried about what it could mean for other immigrants.

“It creates basically a blank check for further indictments of similarly situated people with innocent intent,” she said.

Jamil Ahmad, 51, of Philadelphia, came to the U.S. from Pakistan about a decade ago and claimed asylum. He is now a United States citizen. But in November 2024, he still had his green card. At the time, he said in an interview, get-out-the-vote campaigners were contacting him by mail, by phone and in person, encouraging him to register.

Mr. Ahmad reasoned that if were not allowed to cast a ballot, then the government would not let him. And he considered it his duty to vote, he said. He helped his wife, Nighat Jamil, a 47-year-old permanent legal resident, to register alongside him.

“I was thinking that, if I’m eligible, then they will accept the form,” he said. “If I’m not eligible, they will send me the form back.”

What came in the mail was not a rejection, but a ballot. Mr. Ahmad voted for President Trump. Ms. Jamil, whose English skills are more limited than her husband’s, said that she trusted him to fill out her ballot.

In September, Mr. Ahmad was charged with voting as an alien in a federal election. The authorities came to his house to question him, he said, which spiked his stress levels. But after a couple of weeks, Mr. Ahmad thought it made sense to take responsibility for what had happened.

“When I read all the things,” he said, “now I understand that this is a crime.”

He pleaded guilty last month and is scheduled to be sentenced in January.

Ms. Jamil was also charged with the same voting misdemeanor. She has a court hearing scheduled for this month and is nervous, she said, because she is not a citizen and could be at risk of deportation.

That makes Mr. Ahmad feel sick with guilt, and concerned for his four children.

“I’m just worried,” he said. “How I can look after them if they deport my wife?”

Kirsten Noyes and Seamus Hughes contributed research. Sameen Amin contributed translation.

item.title: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Intervene in California Ballot Case
item.description:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to require that California set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots that the administration claims have been provided to noncitizens.

The emergency application to the justices came after a divided federal appeals court rejected the administration’s arguments that California officials should impound the ballots for further scrutiny.

Legal experts have been skeptical of the Trump administration’s arguments in the case. Filing just one day before the midterm elections may forestall a ruling in the case — and a potential loss for the administration — until after Election Day.

The request requires the Supreme Court to consider how much power the federal government has to order states to make last-minute changes to their vote-counting procedures. Under the Constitution, states have responsibility for administering elections. The Justice Department has claimed that it is empowered by a federal law that makes it illegal for noncitizens to cast ballots.

In their emergency application, lawyers for the administration urged the justices to grant what they called a “modest remedy,” requiring California to separate ballots of “citizens and suspected noncitizens.” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote that such an order by the court “would not cancel any vote but would allow time to verify the eligibility of suspected noncitizens.”

The legal challenge to 20,000 California ballots is part of a broader effort by the administration to argue that the elections could be marred by illegal votes by noncitizens. The effort comes as polls show Republicans could lose control of one or both chambers of Congress and as President Trump has sought to cast doubt on the validity of the vote, despite little evidence of widespread problems with illegal voting. California officials have said the voter list provided by the Trump administration is filled with errors.

The solicitor general appeared to distance the lawyers in his office, an elite division of the Justice Department that represents the federal government before the Supreme Court, from direct knowledge of whether the people on the list were actually noncitizens.

Mr. Sauer wrote that his office “has been informed that the United States has identified more than 20,000 individuals” who appeared to be registered to vote in California and who “in the United States’ view, are likely not U.S. citizens.”

The emergency application was assigned to Justice Elena Kagan, who handles such petitions from that region of the country and can choose to refer the matter to the full court. It was not clear how quickly she intended to act or whether the justices would take up the application before Election Day.

One elections law expert, Richard L. Hasen, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, called the administration’s move an “emergency Hail Mary petition” that was unlikely to succeed.

As the lawsuit has wound through the lower courts, the administration has also threatened criminal charges over claims of noncitizens voting, including charging 28 people with violating federal election laws and subpoenaing county election workers in California.

The Justice Department sent the list of 20,000 names to Los Angeles County elections officials in October, claiming that those ballots should be separated because the names had been flagged through a government process as potential noncitizens. Officials have been vague about exactly how the list was prepared, and county officials have said that the list appeared to include people with addresses throughout California. Only 7,035 names on the list sent to Los Angeles were listed with addresses in Los Angeles County. Officials confirmed others were born in the United States and were citizens.

Shortly after, the Justice Department sued to stop the counting of mail-in ballots sent to people on the list until their citizenship could be verified.

On Friday, a divided three-judge panel on a federal appeals court rejected arguments by the Justice Department to segregate the contested ballots, finding that the administration had overstepped its bounds by interfering with the state’s role in setting its election rules. The panel also cited a principle repeatedly upheld by the Supreme Court that federal courts should avoid ordering changes to how ballots are counted too close to an election.

That same panel of federal judges had already rejected an appeal in the same case earlier in the week, declining to leapfrog a trial judge.

That judge, David O. Carter, then sided with California officials, writing that the federal government’s request could “wreak havoc” on state election administration and “create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike.”

item.title: Who Is Jason Turkish, Haley Stevens’s Fiancé?
item.description:
Even before the Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens scrambled Michigan’s U.S. Senate race on Sunday by endorsing the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, another man in her orbit had garnered increased attention: Jason Turkish, her fiancé.

Mr. Turkish said last Wednesday that he would not support the Democratic Party’s nominee for U.S. Senate, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, over his criticisms of Israel. Then, on Sunday, Ms. Stevens threw her support behind Mr. Rogers after joining him for services at a prominent Black church in Detroit, despite previous assurances to Democratic leaders that she would support her party’s ticket.

The feud between Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed — and the role that Mr. Turkish may have played in the intraparty spat — underlines how the debate over U.S. support of Israel has roiled Democratic politics.

Here’s what else we know.

Mr. Turkish, 39, is a lawyer and fund-raiser for Democratic candidates and Jewish causes. He is based in Southfield, a suburb of Detroit, and graduated from the University of Michigan in 2007, the same year as Dr. El-Sayed. He is also the president and managing partner of Nyman Turkish, a disability rights firm. He has been legally blind since birth.

Mr. Turkish is a longtime political donor. A self-proclaimed “lifelong Democrat,” he and his firm have given money to multiple Democratic campaigns across the country but he has also donated to at least one Republican, Senator Susan Collins of Maine, according to federal records.

Former Gov. James Blanchard of Michigan, a close friend of Ms. Stevens’s, described Mr. Turkish as “a real political junkie” who has raised a lot of money for Democratic candidates in the state. He is also active in the state’s Jewish and pro-Israel circles and is a donor to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. He has relatives who live and were born in Israel.

Mr. Turkish and Ms. Stevens met after the 2022 midterm elections through a mutual friend. They bonded as they discussed her disability rights legislation, she said in interviews, and their conversations about policy evolved into a romantic relationship. They announced their engagement in August, shortly after Ms. Stevens lost the primary election to Dr. El-Sayed.

“We just fell in love,” Ms. Stevens told The Detroit News in August. “We had years of just friendship and conversation, and we have a lot of shared values and commitment to family and friends in Michigan.”

The couple vacationed in Italy and Israel after sharing the news of their engagement. Ms. Stevens has said she has met with a rabbi to discuss converting to Judaism before they get married next summer.

In the final week of the campaign, Mr. Turkish said he would vote for Mr. Rogers because he felt Dr. El-Sayed had not sufficiently moderated his views on Israel. Mr. Turkish attended an event for the Republican Jewish Coalition supporting Mr. Rogers shortly after endorsing him.

“I watched Haley graciously concede an election, and open her arms and her heart to Abdul on Aug. 5, the day after the primary, and I prayed that he would moderate, and he hasn’t,” he said in an interview before the event.

On Friday Mr. Turkish appeared on TMZ to explain his support for Mr. Rogers, pointing to a digital advertisement from supporters of Dr. El-Sayed that blames rising grocery prices in the United States on its support for Israel’s military campaign. He called on Dr. El-Sayed to disavow the ad and suggested that if he did not, Ms. Stevens would not support him. Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign sought to distance the candidate from the ad, saying that it was created by a left-wing political action committee, Rebellion PAC, and was “not affiliated in any way” with him or his candidacy.

On Sunday, when Ms. Stevens appeared alongside Mr. Rogers at the Perfecting Church in Detroit, Mr. Turkish was also in attendance.

item.title: We Talked to 28,000 Voters, and Some Clear Themes Emerged
item.description:
In the run-up to Election Day, people have looked to polls for indications of how the contest for control of Congress may play out. But beyond the horse race, polls this fall have sent some clear messages about what voters care about.

This year, the Times/Siena Poll made nearly four million phone calls to 1.6 million voters, completing more than 28,000 interviews. We will find out on Tuesday how accurate the polls were by our team and by other pollsters across the country, but there are issues on which voters’ opinions are consistent enough that the lead extends well beyond the margin of error. Those issues help shed light on the current political environment and the motivations behind various midterm election decisions.

Polls have consistently shown that the top issue for voters this year is the economy. Every Times/Siena poll conducted in 2026 has found voters listing it as their single biggest driver.

The economy was also a top issue in the 2024 presidential election, but in a departure from recent years, voters are placing their trust in Democrats this time. Nationally, they favor Democrats to handle the economy over Republicans by eight percentage points. The shift is a reversal from just two years ago, when Donald J. Trump was favored by six points over Kamala Harris on this issue.

Across the seven states in our final battleground poll, six of which Mr. Trump won in 2024, voters were nine percentage points more likely to say they trusted Democrats to handle the cost of living. In Kansas and Texas, both states that the president won by double digits in 2024, Democrats also held a nine-point advantage on the issue.

Regardless of the outcome of the elections on Tuesday, one thing is clear: Voters are frustrated with Mr. Trump. The president’s disapproval rating stands at 60 percent nationally, according to the New York Times presidential approval tracker.

Mr. Trump’s approval rating for his handling of the economy has fallen to 35 percent, a drop from 43 percent in April last year. It is down among men and women; white, Black and Hispanic voters; Democrats, independents and, to a lesser extent, Republicans.

A vast majority of Republicans, however, remain loyal supporters. More than 80 percent of Republicans in the latest Times/Siena poll said they approved of the president’s job performance. Signs of a mass Republican exodus are not there.

Democrats are expected to have a strong year, but polls show that the party should not take that as a positive sign for its political brand.

Only 28 percent of voters said they were satisfied with the Democratic Party in a Times/Siena poll from last month, compared with 36 percent who said the same about the Republican Party.

The dynamic can be seen most acutely in Texas, where a CNN/SSRS poll found James Talarico, the Democratic nominee, leading the Senate race by six percentage points in a state where he was more popular than the party that nominated him. He had positive favorability (44 percent favorable, 43 percent unfavorable) among likely voters, while the Democratic Party in Texas was decidedly underwater (36 percent favorable, 56 percent unfavorable).

For the last two years, the immigration crackdown has dominated the headlines at times. But only 10 percent of voters listed immigration as the top issue motivating their vote this year, down from 15 percent in 2024, and it is mostly Republicans who cite it as an issue.

Trust on the issue has also changed hands. Voters now give Democrats a four-point advantage on trust to handle immigration, after Mr. Trump had an 11-point edge on the issue in 2024.

Voters’ feelings about individual candidates, not just their political parties, have been shown to matter a great deal.

In South Carolina, a recent Times/Siena poll found the race effectively tied between Senator Darline Graham and Annie Andrews in a state that Mr. Trump won by about 18 percentage points in 2024. Candidate quality has seemed to play a major role in making the race so close.

The poll found that supporters of Ms. Andrews, the Democrat, said their top reasons for backing her were related to positive views of her policies or character (and negative views of Ms. Graham). For Ms. Graham, the Republican appointed to the seat after her brother, Lindsey Graham, died this year, voters’ primary reason for backing her was to help the Republican Party. Less than half as many cited her policies.

item.title: In Florida Governor’s Race, Democrats ‘Feeling Like This Is Our Moment’
item.description:
David Jolly, the Democratic nominee for Florida governor, leaped onto a church stage on Sunday and insisted over and over again, with a sense of conviction unusual for Democrats in this Republican state: “We’re going to win this race!”

He sounded more like a preacher than a politician. And, against all odds, he has started to turn some Florida Democrats into believers.

The state has not elected a Democratic governor since 1994. It has become only more Republican over the last eight years, giving the G.O.P. a wide advantage in voter registration. Mr. Jolly has been outraised and outspent by Representative Byron Donalds, his Republican rival, who has the backing of both President Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis, the state’s most popular Republican.

Yet it is Democrats who feel the wind at their backs ahead of Tuesday, at least in the governor’s race. Last week, a New York Times/Siena University poll found Mr. Donalds with only a slim lead in the unexpectedly close race.

At Mr. Jolly’s campaign rally on Sunday, Democrats took the microphone one after the other and said what few of them have dared to imagine for many election cycles now.

“Anybody feeling like this is our moment?” Mayor Eileen Higgins of Miami asked to cheers.

“I am so damn ready,” said Mayor Daniella Levine Cava of Miami-Dade County. “I feel for the first time in about a decade that there is real hope for change.”

Mr. Jolly, a former Republican congressman, campaigns from what he calls the “post-ideological space,” telling voters that he is trying to grow the Democratic coalition by welcoming Republicans and independents looking beyond party labels. The son of a pastor, he speaks about moral values driving public policy for the greater good.

“The new coalition that’s emerging in American politics is actually believing in the fundamental goodness of a nation that should provide opportunity to the most number of people, to build a bigger table and create better opportunity,” he said on Sunday at the Coral Gables Congregational Church.

In the audience were two of the three Democrats running for statewide cabinet positions, and one running for Congress. All were looking for a lift from Mr. Jolly’s campaign.

Some Florida Republicans have started to sound alarms about sluggish turnout.

Mr. DeSantis, the protagonist of many of Florida’s recent Republican victories, warned on Sunday that if G.O.P. lag persisted through Election Day, his party might be in trouble.

“If people stay home, you could end up seeing results that you’re going to be wondering what happened,” he said at a campaign event in West Palm Beach for James Uthmeier, the state’s Republican attorney general. “That’s just the reality.”

When he won re-election by 19 percentage points in 2022, Mr. DeSantis noted, “We had real strong enthusiasm.”

“Now, the atmospherics are different,” he added. “I mean, the reality is, gas is higher. That’s not good. Some of these Republicans that try to act like it’s no big deal, I disagree with that. That is a big deal for people.”

Even in Mr. Trump’s adopted home state, which has looked solidly red, not all Florida Republicans may be able to outrun Mr. Trump’s unpopularity and widespread voter discontent over the high cost of living. Mr. Trump has rallied in the state twice over the past 10 days.

There are also dynamics at play particular to the governor’s race.

Mr. Donalds, who would become Florida’s first Black governor, did not win some largely white, rural counties in North Florida in the August primary election. Some Republicans looked at that underperformance with concern about whether some white Republicans would be willing to vote for a Black nominee in the general election. Mr. Donalds has tried to win crossover votes from Black Democrats, but it is unclear how successful he has been. Mr. Jolly is white.

Meantime, traditional Democratic voters, including young voters and Black voters, appear to be turning out in part thanks to State Representative Angie Nixon, the Democratic Senate nominee.

Ms. Nixon, who is Black, ran a grass-roots campaign drawn from her experience as a union and community organizer that led to a shocking primary win. Democrats privately credit her efforts in the general election with bolstering Mr. Jolly’s chances, even though she may not win her own race. As a former Republican, Mr. Jolly might not have otherwise appealed to some loyal Democrats.

Mr. Jolly has leaned into his political evolution. He does not say that the G.O.P. left him; instead, he says that he spent years as an independent and then found his “political home” in the Democratic Party. When he began to explore a run for governor, he drove to meet party activists across the state. Many later backed him.

“We are a nation that is broken,” he said on Sunday, at times pounding the church lectern.

“Our leaders on the other side keep telling us that if we just stay divided, somehow life’s going to improve,” he added, “and it’s not working.”

item.title: Trump Says a Senator Has a ‘Powerful’ Rear. Will It Help Him Win?
item.description:
There it was. The most famous rear end in politics.

It was hard to see under layers of flannel and quilted vest, but that was definitely it.

The one that President Trump has called a “great ass” and a “pile of muscle.” The one that, as a result, starred on “Saturday Night Live” and blew up on TikTok. The one that belongs to Senator Jon Husted, the Republican candidate in a high-stakes election in Ohio, who for a brief moment at a campaign event on Saturday night turned around onstage.

“We couldn’t see it,” said Missy Hartman, 58, a baker at a grocery store.

“I never check anyone’s butt out,” said Jeff Bair, 73, a farmer.

“It’s a middle-aged ass,” said Karen Tetrick, 52, who owns an apartment complex. “I should know, I have one.”

Here is the thing about Mr. Trump’s comments about Mr. Husted’s rear: Online and across Ohio, they have more people talking about the senator than anyone has in the two years since he was appointed to the Senate to succeed Vice President JD Vance.

Mr. Trump, who first complimented the senator’s backside at a campaign rally last month and has not stopped talking about it since, can be mocking, crass and cruel with his focus of physicality. But in this case, he took a candidate who had toiled in relative anonymity and gave him an identity that stuck.

“I’m jealous,” Mr. Vance said last week on Fox News of Mr. Husted’s rump. “The president has never said that about me.”

Mr. Husted, 59, has leaned into the newfound attention. Before his physique — or rather, a description of his physique — went viral, even some hard-core Republican voters in Ohio had hardly heard of him. Many of them thought his opponent, Sherrod Brown, a Democrat and former senator who has been a fixture in Ohio politics since the 1970s, was still in office.

Now at least some of them know about Mr. Husted’s allegedly powerful glutes. What’s his secret? His staff members declined to share his gym routine. They also declined to let a reporter join him for a workout, citing “trade secrets.”

Mr. Trump has claimed the attention on Mr. Husted’s frame has given the senator a 12-point lift in the polls. A new New York Times and Siena University poll shows Mr. Brown, a longtime economic populist, ahead by six points.

“I know nothing about Jon Husted’s body,” said Judy Kruger, 68, a Republican. “It’s not anything to make me vote one way or another.”

Jason Vannette, 50, who on Friday joined a small group of Democratic protesters outside a rally in Toledo for Republican candidates, sized up Mr. Trump’s remarks this way: “It’s weird.”

For his part, Mr. Husted has played up the president’s commentary.

At the event on Saturday in Fairlawn, he arrived with a football in his hand and kept it with him as he took the microphone and addressed the crowd.

“During the campaign, President Trump discovered that I was a college football player,” said Mr. Husted, who played at the University of Dayton nearly 40 years ago. “He’s been talking about it.”

The senator threw the football into a room of attendees eating apple pie.

There was a reason Mr. Trump said he had been “studying” Mr. Husted’s body.

Republicans in Ohio are trying to turn the Senate race, which could decide control of the chamber, into a culture war much like the ones that delivered Mr. Trump and others on the right to power.

On one side, according to Mr. Husted: socialism, transgender athletes and a world in which Mother’s Day becomes “Birthing Person’s Day.”

On the other? In the words of the president, a former football player with “a big piece of muscle” on his backside.

“I don’t do this with men very often,” Mr. Trump said last month at a rally in Youngstown. “I started examining his body.”

He apparently would like to continue to do so aboard Air Force One. Bill Pulte, a top federal housing official, made a poster of Mr. Husted for the president to display on the plane.

So far, the focus on Mr. Husted’s buttocks appears to have mixed results in Ohio — or at least it did among the voters who convened on Sunday at a bar in Geneva to meet candidates and watch the Cleveland Browns game.

“Who cares?” said Donald Goodenow, 66, a lab tech wearing a Harley-Davidson sweatshirt, when a reporter asked him if he had heard Mr. Trump’s comments about Mr. Husted.

Mr. Goodenow said he thought Mr. Brown was in office and planned to vote for Mr. Husted because “by the looks of most of the Democratic Party, they’re out to lunch.”

Ms. Tetrick said she was considering leaving Mr. Husted’s bubble blank, despite broadly supporting Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.

“Sherrod Brown, I do appreciate him over the years — he did care about the people,” said Ms. Tetrick. “Husted, I just don’t know.”

Mr. Husted was not at the bar on Sunday with the other Republican candidates who had taken a bus to mingle with voters at the sports bar.

Perhaps he was at the gym.

Mack Liederman contributed from Toledo, Ohio.

item.title: Mystery Group Spends Millions to Boost Third-Party Spoilers at Republicans’ Expense
item.description:
About $6.5 million has been spent over the final 10 days of the campaign on mailers and digital ads promoting obscure third-party candidates with almost no chance of winning on Tuesday. What gives?

The material is an apparent “spoiler” effort to persuade voters who are considering backing a Republican to instead support right-wing candidates who would peel away votes from a major party nominee. The final days of campaigns often feature tactics like these, with the belief that futzing around on the margins of a race could be decisive in determining the ultimate winner.

Mailers shared with The New York Times by Mintt, a mail-tracking firm, show some of the subterfuge that appears to be at play from a super PAC called Our Heritage Matters. The PAC was registered on Oct. 15, meaning it is not required to disclose its donors until December. All of its spending has been through two Delaware limited-liability companies that themselves were formed within the last month, on Oct. 6, and have reported no other activity, according to corporate records.

In one of America’s tightest House races in Colorado, a mailer promoting Dave Wood, the Libertarian nominee, says that Representative Gabe Evans, a Republican, has a “liberal agenda” and would “join forces with Socialist Democrats.”

A nearly identical mailer interchanges those names with the Republican nominee, Jennifer Balkcom, and the Libertarian candidate, Travis Groo, in North Carolina’s 11th District.

Our Heritage Matters is also spending to influence voters in Senate races. Michele Tafoya, the Republican nominee for Senate in Minnesota, is also accused of having a “liberal agenda.” Another mailer from the group calls Mark Hackett, the Constitution Party candidate for Senate in South Carolina, “the true conservative” in the race.

On its website, Our Heritage Matters says: “American culture, values, and traditions are worth defending. We stand for the principles that built this nation — and we will not stand by while they are eroded by enemies foreign and domestic.”

The group did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: How a Beleaguered U.S. Cyber Agency Retreated From Election Security Work
item.description:
Two years ago, the government agency at the forefront of election security did what it had done for every federal election cycle since 2018.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency set up a digital and physical war room, to quickly swap insights and intelligence with state and local officials; updated reporters every few hours on problems occurring nationwide; and sought to educate the public about foreign disinformation campaigns and the resiliency of the United States’ voting process.

But on Tuesday the agency, established by President Trump in his first term, will be largely absent from the action, current and former CISA officials say, weakening the federal government’s ability to help states respond to problems ranging from routine vote-machine disruptions to online hoaxes to bad actors looking to undermine public confidence in the vote. Instead, it is expected to offer light assistance to state and local election officials, many of whom fear the federal government is more likely to meddle with election results than to help safeguard them. There will be no scheduled briefings with reporters, an agency spokesman confirmed on Monday.

“The posture seems like the bare minimum,” said Geoff Hale, a former top election security official at CISA. Such an approach to election security, he said, was not well suited to identifying problems that cut across multiple voting jurisdictions or “the type of national security concerns that once drove the mission.”

It is a remarkable retreat from the agency’s history as a loud and visible presence around Election Day across both the first Trump and Biden administrations.

CISA, the cyber wing of the Department of Homeland Security, was a lead federal partner for states on election security efforts after the 2016 election, sharing cybersecurity best practices and intelligence about foreign intentions around elections. The agency’s leadership and election security advisers painstakingly worked to build trusted relationships with Republican, Democratic and nonpartisan state and local officials, eventually smoothing out concerns among many of them worried about federal intervention in elections, which the Constitution says are overseen by individual states.

But Mr. Trump developed disdain for the agency, and for the government’s election security work generally. Its director at the time, Christopher Krebs, validated the integrity of the 2020 election, prompting the president to fire him.

During Mr. Trump’s second term, the agency has been largely rudderless, with no Senate-confirmed leader. It has continued to be sidelined on elections, even as Mr. Trump gave a prime-time address this summer in which he exaggerated claims about election vulnerabilities and vowed to fix security issues.

Much of its work on election security was gutted as the administration systematically dismantled the expertise built up at the agency. Staff reductions and budget cuts hit deeper than at other offices within the Department of Homeland Security or the broader federal government — CISA shed about a third of its work force, which stood at 3,400 in January 2025. In February last year, the administration put more than a dozen CISA election security workers on leave as part of an investigation into its election work, a move that had a chilling effect on the 100 or so people in the division, former officials said.

While CISA has recently hired some new personnel, the jobs are not for election security positions, current and former officials said.

Other federal agencies have also downsized their election security work, including the F.B.I. and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. But CISA, as the public-facing arm of the federal government’s election protection efforts, has made cuts that state and local officials have felt the most.

Among other changes, the agency ended the voluntary cybersecurity reviews it had offered to state and local jurisdictions for election systems. In some locations, though, they continued if local officials requested generic cybersecurity reviews for a courthouse or other state building that housed election tabulation machines, instead of specifically requesting help for an election.

And the regular flow of intelligence warnings, prepared by spy agencies and passed to local officials by CISA, slowed to a trickle, according to election experts.

In a statement, a CISA spokesman said it was “fully equipped and prepared to address any national security cyber threats that face our nation,” and described the agency as “stronger than ever” despite the staff reductions.

“Our regional teams assist partners across the country by assessing risks, helping entities strengthen their defenses and resilience, and responding promptly to threats,” the spokesman said. “As CISA has routinely done for previous elections, the agency has activated an incident coordination group before and on Election Day to support election officials and maintain a unified operational picture.”

CISA is treating the midterm elections as a “one-day hurricane,” said a current official at the agency, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. In practice, that means that regional personnel are expected to be on hand to lend help to states as requested on cybersecurity or physical security issues as they arise. But there is no coordinated national war room effort as there has been during every election cycle since 2018, the official said.

The lack of briefings to the news media will leave a vacuum of reliable federal information on Election Day, former officials and election experts said.

“They don’t have the expertise anymore,” said Mr. Hale, now a visiting fellow on election security at the Center for Democracy & Technology. “But they were a value add amid the fog of an election.”

Officials from the agency note that since Mr. Trump took office, their regional teams have conducted 700 engagements — including planning events, training sessions, and cyber and physical security assessments — with state, local and federal partners. The agency, officials said, continues to pass on warnings and provide technical guidance.

Former officials and election experts said that there was a low bar for what qualified as an “engagement.” Regardless, they added, the figure was low given the number of election jurisdictions nationwide, which some estimates put between 8,000 and 10,000.

Internally, employees acknowledge that little has been done to help states ahead of the midterms, current and former agency officials said. Election experts and local officials say that much of the engagement that took place this year was not helpful for this election, but could potentially be useful for the 2028 presidential election.

In 2020, during the first Trump term, the agency released its election security plan that February. This year, it was issued in late September. It contained minimal information that was new or helpful, election experts said.

In some ways, CISA’s help may be less needed today than in the past. States have improved their election security efforts considerably since revelations of Russian interference operations emerged a decade ago. They also have better protocols today than before Russia sought to interfere in the 2016 election.

But the federal government has returned to its posture before the 2016 cycle, former CISA officials said, no longer regularly sharing intelligence with states about foreign threats or convening election officials to address local and state issues as they arose.

“While the federal government may be back to its 2016 understanding of elections, states aren’t there — they are better postured to defend themselves,” Mr. Hale said. “There are more paper ballots than ever. There are more controls than ever. But that means that the one area that’s at its weakest is the cyberthreat information sharing, the understanding of adversaries and sharing of information about their plans and intentions.”

A recent interview with Nick Andersen, who is serving as both the acting director of CISA and its deputy director, underscored the agency’s rapid shift in approach under the second Trump administration.

Mr. Andersen, appearing on a podcast late last month to discuss the agency’s new cyber strategy, spoke for 10 minutes about its focus on protecting U.S. critical infrastructure. He discussed many aspects of CISA’s mission, including partnerships with the private sector, improving national resiliency to physical and cyber threats, and the integrity of essential services.

He made no mention of the election.

item.title: Judge Dismisses Trump Lawsuit Demanding Harvard Admissions Data
item.description:
A federal judge granted Harvard University’s motion to dismiss a Trump administration lawsuit that sought to force the school to turn over admissions documents for a government discrimination investigation.

The administration sued Harvard in February, accusing the university of trying to stymie a federal review of the school’s admissions procedures by withholding documents that the government wanted — among them, application essays written by individual students.

Harvard “slow-walked the pace of production” of documents and refused to provide others related to applicant-level admissions decisions, the administration said in its suit.

A federal district judge in Boston, Myong J. Joun, wrote in an order on Monday that the administration had not cleared procedural hurdles to satisfy a court order for the materials.

“The ruling does not determine whether Harvard has discriminated, whether the agencies may lawfully seek appropriately defined applicant-level data, or whether Harvard may ultimately be required to provide such data,” the judge wrote.

The university, in court filings, said the administration’s demands went too far. The school portrayed the lawsuit as “part of the Trump administration’s ongoing campaign against Harvard” to try to force it into negotiations. The school has said that it has complied with federal law in its admissions processes.

Harvard did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. Trump officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Michael C. Bender contributed reporting.

item.title: Former Head of Chicago F.B.I. Sues Justice Department Over Resignation
item.description:
The former head of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Chicago field office sued the Department of Justice on Monday, saying he was forced out of his job and used as a “scapegoat” for Andrew S. Boutros, the U.S. attorney in Chicago.

Douglas DePodesta, who abruptly resigned in July, named Mr. Boutros as a defendant in the lawsuit, accusing him of spearheading politically motivated prosecutions of protesters during the Trump administration’s 2025 immigration crackdown in Illinois and then blaming Mr. DePodesta when those cases fell apart.

Mr. Boutros engineered Mr. DePodesta’s resignation by telling his superiors at the Justice Department that Mr. DePodesta had “conspired to destroy” one case against a group of protesters known as the Broadview Six, the lawsuit said.

“To deflect attention from his own malfeasance, Boutros began a campaign within the Department of Justice to blame DePodesta for the unraveling of the case,” the lawsuit said.
