item.title: In Run-Up to Midterms, Legacy of 2020 Looms Large Over Justice Dept.
item.description:
Senior leaders of the Justice Department, many of them veterans of President Trump’s legal and political wars over the past decade, share a singular, striking attribute: They have not admitted, unequivocally or plainly, that he lost the 2020 election.

Attorney General Todd Blanche; his predecessor, Pam Bondi; the F.B.I. director, Kash Patel; and Harmeet K. Dhillon, the head of the department’s civil rights division, have all avoided providing yes-or-no answers about the election in appearances before Congress. Instead, they have acknowledged only that President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory was legally certified.

Emil Bove III, a former Blanche aide, offered a telling non-answer during his confirmation process for a federal judgeship last year: It was inappropriate to opine on 2020 because it was an unresolved “political or policy debate,” he wrote in a questionnaire.

This refusal to acknowledge the fact that Mr. Trump lost, a go-to tactic for nominees seeking to avoid contradicting the president, has become so commonplace it no longer warrants much attention. Yet it reflects the enduring legacy of a polarizing election whose reverberations are still being felt, perhaps most consequentially in the department’s presumption that voter fraud is so rampant that it requires a forceful federal response. That premise has been challenged by state election officials and expert analysis.

“This is a different approach than we have seen in any previous Department of Justice, whether it was run by Republicans or Democrats,” said Karen Brinson Bell, the former executive director of the North Carolina State Board of Elections.

Ms. Brinson Bell said the administration’s current initiatives, like its attempt to curtail mail-in voting, the unsuccessful effort to obtain sensitive voter data from states and the issuance of threats against local officials, underscore themes Mr. Trump struck six years ago.

The 2020 election “seems to have been something of a catalyst” for their current actions, she added.

Mr. Trump built a powerhouse political movement by mobilizing supporters to align with his grievances, including his debunked claims of a conspiracy to steal the election and his rage over being prosecuted for his role in inciting the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

And the president has explicitly linked his stop-the-steal message six years ago to the midterm elections this year.

He exploded after a federal court recently rejected the department’s demand that officials in California stop counting 20,000 mail-in ballots over concerns the batch included noncitizens who voted illegally, even though such instances are exceedingly rare.

“Why would they reject fixing Election Fraud?” Mr. Trump wrote on social media on Saturday as he continued to stew over the Supreme Court’s refusal to consider his efforts to overturn the 2020 results.

“That’s like, in the 2020 Rigged and Stolen Election, when we had a great case, but the Supreme Court would not hear it because they said I, the President of the United States of America, had NO STANDING to bring such a case.”

This spring, Mr. Blanche, the president’s former defense lawyer, told Fox News that “there is a ton of evidence the election was rigged.” But he added that producing evidence that would hold up in court was “very difficult because they’re very good at hiding misconduct and hiding what they’re doing.”

Kiersten Pels, a Justice Department spokeswoman, dismissed the idea that the department’s actions in California and its effort to pre-emptively contest the results of the Alaska’s Senate race were impelled by any lingering grievances over 2020, just the determination to enforce laws the Biden administration would not.

“The Justice Department is focused on 2026 and on enforcing the federal laws that protect it,” Ms. Pels said. “Noncitizen voting is a federal crime. Prosecuting those cases is not ‘interceding’ in state elections. It is the job.”

If the department is facing criticism from the left for doing far too much, some on the right believe Mr. Blanche and his team are doing far too little.

Stephen K. Bannon, the former Trump aide who has long maintained that the 2020 election was stolen, said most of the department’s recent actions were aimed at keeping his boss happy, not at uncovering what he has said is a vast conspiracy to undermine Mr. Trump.

“Everything D.O.J. is doing is totally performative to give some patina of action,” he said in an interview. “Their heart isn’t in it. They slapped together a plan in the last 60 days after Trump started to really tune in.”

Several figures who played central roles in the post-2020 fight have emerged as influential voices in Mr. Trump’s ear. He recently met with Tina Peters, a former election official in Colorado who served prison time for breaching a county voting system. She has urged him to use the power of federal law enforcement to aggressively investigate elections without seeking court orders or the cooperation of state officials.

“He already has the authority to do all this — he doesn’t have to go to Congress to ask,” she told MS NOW on Monday. “If there’s something that is criminal in nature, he has every right to have the administration, the attorney general’s office or, you know, law enforcement go in and investigate.”

The assumptions undergirding the department’s two main lines of legal attack — the effort to sequester ballots based on contested assertions of illegal voting and the intervention, at Mr. Trump’s request, in the Alaska race — echo the drumbeat of 2020 election denialism.

“State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America,” Mr. Blanche said after suing California on Oct. 15. The move kicked off a period of litigation so intense that his tiny team of deputies has had to work around the clock to keep up with the demands of drafting the paperwork.

The effort, he added, was essential to “restore trust in American elections.”

Critics say it was aimed at achieving exactly the opposite, part of a determined political effort to undermine faith in elections — and one destined to fail in court.

“We’re seeing the same unsuccessful playbook as we did in 2020,” said Sam Oliker-Friedland, a former trial lawyer in the voting rights section of the department’s civil rights division. “It’s clear they haven’t learned that much.”

The federal judge in the California case, David O. Carter, rejected the department’s argument. He accused the administration of seeking to “disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.”

The department’s appeals in the case have thus far proved unsuccessful. On Monday, it petitioned the Supreme Court to uphold the suit.

The lawsuit embodied the evolution of the Trump administration’s strategy. It has shifted away from investigating broad-based claims of rampant voter fraud that William P. Barr, Mr. Trump’s attorney general during the 2020 election, dismissed as “completely bogus.”

Mr. Blanche and his team have coordinated closely with the Department of Homeland Security to target illegal voting by undocumented immigrants. That approach dovetails with the all-encompassing crackdown on immigration led by Mr. Trump’s top domestic adviser, Stephen Miller.

In the past nine weeks alone, the department has charged 192 immigrants across 26 states with illegal voting and registration offenses. Since the beginning of this administration, the department has charged 236 people with voting-fraud-related offenses, Ms. Pels said.

Another approach with shades of 2020 has been the department’s targeting of state and local election workers. Six years ago, Mr. Trump and his allies accused poll workers in Georgia and elsewhere of intentionally mishandling ballots. In October, the department sent warning letters and subpoenas to officials in California, accusing them of failing to comply with their demands.

On Friday, a federal judge in San Francisco ordered the department not to “threaten, intimidate or coerce state or local elections officials” based on the government’s suspicion a voter might be a noncitizen. She scheduled a hearing for Monday.

Mr. Blanche’s team has said its actions are necessary to safeguard the process. The flurry of 11th-hour activity, they have claimed, represents the urgency of addressing the threat posed by illegal voting with a goal of reminding local officials of their legal obligation to preserve records for future scrutiny.

Mr. Blanche has repeatedly offered assurances that the department’s recent activity was motivated by evidence, not politics. Last month, he told reporters the department would never “improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process.”

In the meantime, dodging questions about the 2020 election remains the go-to tactic of those seeking positions of power in the administration.

“Who won the 2020 election?” Senator Jon Ossoff, a Georgia Democrat, asked Jay Clayton, Mr. Trump’s nominee to be director of national intelligence, during his confirmation hearing in July.

“I’m not going to do this with you,” said Mr. Clayton, who was the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan before he was confirmed.

Mr. Ossoff persisted.

Mr. Clayton repeated that Mr. Biden had been certified the winner.

item.title: Trump’s Election Fraud Reward Raises Fears of Vigilantism, Local Officials Say
item.description:
Local law enforcement and election officials are bracing for a tense Election Day as President Trump has kept up a sustained attack on the integrity of U.S. elections, including by offering a $1 million reward for information that leads to an election fraud conviction.

In response to Mr. Trump’s unsubstantiated claims about voting problems and his campaign to assert more federal control over state-run elections, officials have prepared for potential worst-case scenarios in which the federal government tries to intervene in voting.

Now some local authorities have said they also fear that the president’s offer of a large financial incentive could foster unrest or even vigilantism, with Americans eying one another with suspicion as they head to the polls.

“Don’t drag in the public and basically a vigilante-type system where we’re going to say, ‘Hey, you can make a million dollars here by going over here and accusing somebody of fraud,’” said Sheriff Chris Nanos of Pima County, Ariz., a Democrat. “Our elections are handled at the local level, but yet we have fire and brimstone, if you will, coming down from the federal level.”

Mr. Trump’s unfounded claims that the election could be rigged come at a time when violent threats against public officials and election workers have increasingly become a new normal. To prepare for Tuesday, election officials and local law enforcement agencies have held hundreds of exercises to anticipate a variety of possible threats and disruptions at polling sites.

Chief Chris Davis, who leads the police department in Green Bay, Wis., said the level of fear surrounding elections has increased in recent years, particularly in his battleground state.

“I worry about disturbances at polling places, and we’ve developed pretty comprehensive plans for that if it happens,” said Chief Davis, who added that he was concerned Mr. Trump’s reward offer could further heighten tensions at polling sites.

“If one voter challenges another voter, the potential for that to turn into a disturbance and a big problem for us is very real,” he said.

Deidre Henderson, the Republican lieutenant governor of Utah, has also warned in recent weeks that the federal government has contributed to a tense environment for the midterms.

Ms. Henderson told CBS News’s “60 Minutes” that in previous elections, “the threats were all external: nonstate actors, cybersecurity threats and other things. But now we also have threats coming from within our own government.”

The atmosphere is already fraught. The Justice Department has asked California to set aside 20,000 mail ballots, claiming they were provided to likely noncitizens. The administration has also sought to pre-emptively challenge the results of the Senate race in Alaska, where two candidates named Dan Sullivan are on the ballot. So far, the courts have blocked those efforts.

State and local officials have responded to Mr. Trump’s attacks by seeking to create guardrails to prevent potential disruptions.

Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, a Democrat, sent an extraordinary “alert” on Saturday to the four U.S. district courts that cover California, warning the judges that the Trump administration may try to seize ballots.

And in response to the Justice Department’s plan to dispatch 1,000 federal monitors across the country, some local officials have issued statements saying that monitors are prohibited from crossing into an established perimeter surrounding polling locations, citing state law.

Justin Elicker, the Democratic mayor of New Haven, Conn., said the Justice Department told local officials last month that it would be sending two teams of two people to polling sites in the city to ensure New Haven was complying with federal voting requirements on language assistance and disability access.

The city responded by sending the Justice Department a letter saying the monitors were not welcome to enter any polling locations.

“They intimidate people not to vote,” Mr. Elicker said in an interview. “We would prefer that they not be here.”

In discussions with local and state officials, the Justice Department committed to monitoring from outside a 75-foot perimeter, like other observers, and pledged not to interfere with voting, according to Stephanie Thomas, Connecticut’s Democratic secretary of the state.

A Justice Department spokeswoman said federal monitors do not require approval from state or local authorities but added that monitors are trained to follow local laws that govern access at polling sites.

In the final stretch of the midterm campaign, Mr. Trump has continued to make unsubstantiated claims that the country’s elections can be manipulated, falsely asserting that there is widespread fraud.

“I’m also going to be issuing a $1 million bonus or reward, or whatever you want to call it, for anybody that reports voter fraud, leading to the arrest and conviction of somebody,” Mr. Trump told reporters last week before flying to Mississippi for a campaign rally.

The president has said the offer applies to past elections, as well as the midterms.

Mr. Trump’s dangling of a $1 million reward caps a year in which he has trained the full arsenal of his administration on sowing doubt about the country’s election systems.

The White House declined to answer questions about what money would be used to pay for the reward or how Americans should report fraud, and did not address criticism that the financial incentive could spur people to vigilantism.

Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said that Democrats were the ones eroding election security. “They refused to enact common-sense election security measures like voter ID and citizenship verification,” she said in a statement. “President Trump is right: We have to have honest elections.”

Despite the inflamed rhetoric, local and state officials said that the authorities tasked with ensuring a safe election are prepared for this moment.

“A lot of what has been said has been designed to provoke and cause fear, so we’re paying attention to it but we’re not going to overreact,” said Aghogho Edevbie, the deputy secretary of state of Michigan, who said that his office has helped conduct about 125 security exercises this cycle.

“That is going to cause us to be ready for anything that comes along,” said Mr. Edevbie, a Democrat. “You could ask, ‘Was that more preparation because of what’s happening from D.C.?’ Absolutely.”

Gowri Ramachandran, the director of elections and security in the Brennan Center’s Elections and Government Program, said Americans should not lose faith in poll workers.

“Election officials just really have been working super hard to provide a free and fair election for voters,” Ms. Ramachandran said. “The rhetoric that we see coming out of the administration just does not square with the reality of what election officials and voters are doing. And I would say the only way all of that rhetoric works is if people don’t exercise their rights to vote.”

Nearly three-quarters of voters said they largely trusted that the results of Tuesday’s election would be accurate, including large majorities of Democrats, Republicans and independents, according to a recent New York Times/Siena poll. Still, half of likely voters were worried about Republicans trying to overturn the outcome of the election, while 31 percent of voters were worried about the possibility of Democrats taking such action.

Chuck Wexler, the executive director of the Police Executive Research Forum, which advises departments on best practices, said that current and former police chiefs discussed at a recent gathering how the political divisiveness at the national level had trickled down to communities trying to prepare for the election.

“There are some people who are willing to go beyond rhetoric to actual exercise violence, and that has not been lost on police chiefs,” Mr. Wexler said, noting the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the U.S. Capitol by supporters of Mr. Trump who were angry about the outcome of the 2020 election. “What used to be a simple constitutional right of voting now has become an issue of considerable agitation.”

Neil Vigdor, Devlin Barrett and Eileen Sullivan contributed reporting.

item.title: Just Tuning Into the Midterms? Here’s What to Know About the Fight for Congress.
item.description:
The United States has reached the midterm elections, and voters will have an opportunity to deliver a judgment on the country’s direction two years into President Trump’s second term.

Mr. Trump enters the midterms on Tuesday with his approval rating near its lowest level ever, dragged down by the unpopular war in Iran and rising consumer prices that have outpaced wages and left many Americans struggling to cover their basic needs.

The president’s diminished standing and the country’s gloomy mood have given Democrats hope that voters will hand them majorities in Congress, which is controlled by Republicans.

More often than not, the party that controls the White House loses seats in the midterms. From 1934 to 2022, the president’s party bled an average of 27 seats in the House and three in the Senate, according to the American Presidency Project at the University of California, Santa Barbara.

This year, strategists in both parties say it is likely that Democrats will wrest back the 435-seat House, offering the party a check on the Trump administration. But the picture in the 100-seat Senate is more complicated.

Here’s what to know.

Both parties see the battle for the Senate as a tossup, and recent polling has encouraged Democrats.

In this chamber, where lawmakers serve six-years terms and only 35 of 100 seats are on the ballot, Democrats have a more challenging path than they do in the House.

Democrats’ route to a Senate majority goes through a number of states that are traditionally Republican strongholds.

Democrats hold 47 Senate seats. To take back the chamber, they must flip at least four seats held by Republicans. At the same time, Democrats are trying to defend seats in two states Mr. Trump won in 2024. And five of the seven most competitive Senate races are in states that Mr. Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

The seven most competitive races are in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas.

Early this year, even the most optimistic Democrats viewed their chances of winning back the Senate as low, given the daunting map. But then Mr. Trump took the country to war, and the conflict clogged a vital oil-shipping corridor, sending the price of gasoline and diesel soaring. Rising shipping costs made myriad goods more expensive, upending Mr. Trump’s vows to make America “affordable again.”

Democrats have campaigned on promises to curb inflation and end the war. Although the party is still viewed skeptically by much of the public, according to opinion polls, the message has appeared to resonate.

Now polls suggest Democrats are ahead in almost all of the key Senate battlegrounds. Still, polls are imperfect, and some Democrats have sought to manage expectations, cognizant that they must overcome a challenging partisan tilt in many of those states.

More than in the Senate, races in the House tend to closely follow the national mood. Americans often vote for parties rather than specific candidates when they elect representatives, who serve two-year terms and are on the ballot every election cycle.

This year, the powerful political headwinds facing Republicans have left them with long odds of keeping the chamber. At the moment, Republicans have a razor-thin advantage in the House: 218 seats to 214 seats.

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, projects that Democrats will flip between 12 and 25 seats and finish with up to 240 seats.

The vast majority of the most competitive House races are playing out in districts held by Republicans.

The national House battle was reshaped earlier this year, after Republicans, urged on by Mr. Trump, redrew congressional district lines to advantage their party, starting in Texas.

Democrats fought back, redrawing districts in blue states such as California, but in some cases they were foiled by courts. In the end, Republicans emerged from the redistricting war with a structural advantage, aided by a Supreme Court decision that weakened the Voting Rights Act and allowed them to redraw more districts.

Still, that edge is seen as unlikely to be enough for Republicans to keep the House in a difficult political climate.

Mr. Trump has spent weeks crisscrossing the country, delivering an unusual midterm pitch.

“Pretend I’m on the ballot, because essentially I am on the ballot,” Mr. Trump pleaded at a rally Sunday in Iowa, a Senate battleground. The line invariably appears in his long, winding and often unscripted speeches.

It’s the same message Democrats are relaying to voters.

Unpopular presidents don’t typically try to make midterms referendums of their presidencies. But Mr. Trump and his advisers are hoping to juice turnout among Americans who don’t always vote but turned out to elect him to the White House in 2016 and 2024.

Democrats have prosecuted a case that Mr. Trump has made America unaffordable and lost touch with the needs of voters. They have accused his administration of corruption and described the Iran war as ill-planned and unnecessary. They have pilloried the president’s efforts to make over Washington and renovate the White House, saying that they are gaudy vanity projects.

“He should be on HGTV,” former President Barack Obama said at a rally in Ohio in October, mocking Mr. Trump. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”

Republicans have also sought to persuade voters that Democratic candidates are unacceptable options, casting them as politically extreme — and sometimes worse. The strategy has produced one of the darkest elections in modern American history, as Republicans have attacked Democrats with false and incendiary claims.

item.title: What Voters Should Know About Possible Problems at the Polls
item.description:
Americans will head to polling sites on Tuesday after a year in which President Trump has used the levers of the federal government to bolster unsubstantiated claims of election fraud.

Many election officials and Democrats have said they fear that the president’s attacks on the integrity of elections could lead to tensions as people vote, and to baseless challenges of the outcome. Local and state officials have even incorporated planning for potential federal intervention into their preparations for Election Day.

Nevertheless, it remains to be seen whether any worst-case scenarios will play out. And state and local authorities have emphasized that they are well prepared to help run a fair and safe election.

“The election officials in this country, the law enforcement in this country and other stakeholders are doing everything they possibly can to make sure that Election Day goes off without a hitch,” said Tina Barton, the co-chairwoman of the Committee for Safe and Secure Elections, an organization that has helped conduct election training sessions around the country. “Any incident that does happen is quickly mitigated because they already have a game plan for it.”

Here’s what voters should know:

Mr. Trump has notably refused to rule out invoking the Insurrection Act, in connection with the election. The 1807 law gives the president broad authority, under some conditions, to use the military to quell widespread domestic unrest. The extreme move has been encouraged by some of the president’s outside supporters.

In late August, however, the president’s top military adviser, Gen. Dan Caine, said there were no plans for the armed forces to deploy troops in relation to the elections. “I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order concerning the role of the Joint Force in the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections,” he wrote in a letter to a Democratic senator.

Legal experts say federal laws also prohibit troops or armed officials from being deployed to polling sites, even if Mr. Trump were to cite the Insurrection Act. “Federal law unambiguously prohibits the presence of armed federal officers at the polls, unless necessary to repel an armed attack by foreign enemies,” according to the Brennan Center for Justice.

Some voting rights advocates have also grown concerned about the prospect of Mr. Trump’s deploying Immigration and Customs Enforcement or other federal agents to polling sites. The Homeland Security Department has played a leading role in trying to find noncitizen voters to support the president’s false claims of widespread illegal voting.

But federal officials have downplayed that idea. Speaking to reporters in September, Markwayne Mullin, Mr. Trump’s homeland security secretary, said it was not the job of immigration agents to patrol polling places. He said they would be dispatched only “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down.”

Some election experts have noted that ICE agents are regularly dispatched on American streets as a part of their routine work, and that the mere sight of them near polling places could lead to misreporting on social media and cause fears among voters. They encourage members of the public to report concerns to poll workers or to election hotlines.

The Justice Department expects to have roughly 1,000 election monitors deployed in all 50 states on Election Day, according to Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the department’s civil rights unit. That is an expansion of past efforts, in which a smaller number monitors focused on states and city jurisdictions with a history of voting problems.

In an interview in August with Bloomberg, Ms. Dhillon said that the monitors would be deployed to places “where there may be language issues, the places where there may have been access of disability rights issues, places where there may be voter fraud issues that we’ve seen.”

The overall goal, she said, is “increasing all American citizens’ confidence in our elections.”

The large deployment by the Justice Department, which has promoted contested claims about election fraud and sought to preemptively challenge the results in the Alaska Senate race, has worried some local election officials. In recent days, some jurisdictions have issued statements saying that monitors are prohibited from crossing into an established perimeter surrounding polling locations, citing state law. Those laws vary by jurisdiction.

A Justice Department spokeswoman said that federal monitors did not require approval from state or local authorities, but added that monitors were trained to follow local laws that govern access at polling sites.

The Justice Department monitors will also not be authorized to make any arrests, a department lawyer said on Monday at a court hearing in Washington.

In nearly every place in the country, Justice Department monitors must follow the state regulations that apply to any visitors to polling places, including prohibitions on interfering with voters or intimidating them, said Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University who formerly worked as an adviser on voting rights in the Biden White House.

The rules are different for a separate category of federal observers, he added: monitors sent by the U.S. House of Representatives. Those observers have also been present at U.S. polling places for decades. Their job, according to the Committee on House Administration, which provides credentials to the observers, is to “ensure that conduct of the election was free and fair.”

Election machines are heavily monitored and regulated through testing and certification by federal agencies, states, local election offices and private labs.

In recent elections, however, rumors about “vote flipping,” in which voters’ choices are incorrectly logged, have gone viral on social media.

Election officials say that many of these problems are the result of user error. A recent examination of the issue by PolitiFact determined that “there is no evidence of voting machines deliberately designed with such flaws or that it is happening on a wide scale.”

“Historically, these types of rumors emerge from poorly designed or malfunctioning interfaces (and occasionally user error) but are often misleadingly framed as intentional attempts to switch votes instead of rare errors with remedies,” according to the Election Rumor Research team at the University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public.

Still, Mr. Trump and top administration officials have continuously promoted false claims that voting machines can be manipulated. Earlier this year, Mr. Mullin asked the Justice Department to examine whether a commonly used voting machine could be trusted. And Mr. Trump last month met with Tina Peters, a former Colorado county clerk who was convicted of tampering with voting machines after the 2020 election. Ms. Peters has called on Mr. Trump to inspect or seize voting machines — a move that legal experts say would be an overreach of federal authority.

Election experts said the public should be wary about any claims they see online about widespread irregularities with voting machines.

“It’s really important, first things first, for people to not spread unverified reports on social media about things that they’re seeing,” said Gowri Ramachandran, the director of elections and security at the Brennan Center for Justice. “It’s much better to, you know, let a poll worker know.”

Devlin Barrett and Eileen Sullivan contributed reporting.

item.title: Grand Jury Rejects Bid by Justice Dept. to Bring Charges Over Voter Fraud
item.description:
A federal grand jury in Washington on Friday rejected an effort by the Justice Department to indict an individual for voter fraud who prosecutors claimed voted in two jurisdictions during the 2024 election, according to four people briefed on the matter.

The rejection, along with a string of losses the Justice Department has been handed in courts across the country in recent weeks, demonstrates the department’s harried push to prove President Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of rampant voter fraud.

It also shows the increasing difficulty federal prosecutors in Washington have faced in bringing indictments on a range of matters, including against Mr. Trump’s perceived political enemies. Last week, a grand jury declined to indict Cassidy Hutchinson, a former Trump aide who had been in the president’s cross hairs after she gave damning testimony about him involving the Capitol riot on Jan. 6, 2021.

Grand jury proceedings are held in secret, leaving it uncertain why jurors rejected the case. And there were differing accounts about why prosecutors brought this case, particularly so close to the midterm election. Previous Justice Departments shied away from bringing politically fraught cases in the weeks before Election Day to avoid the appearance of trying to tip the scales.

According to one person familiar with the matter, the case was brought in response to pressure from political appointees, including the U.S. attorney in Washington, Jeanine Pirro, who wanted to follow through on Mr. Trump’s demands to bring cases involving potential voter fraud as the midterms neared.

Another person familiar with the case said that the investigation had been opened after the District of Columbia Board of Elections sent the U.S. attorney’s office a list of several people whom they found had voted twice.

A spokesman for the U.S. attorney’s office in Washington did not return a request for comment.

Bringing voter fraud indictments would have armed Mr. Trump with a fresh example he could point to as he seeks to undermine the public’s faith in the election results.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly made false claims of widespread voter fraud and the Justice Department, acting on his orders, has filed a flurry of criminal cases across the country in recent weeks. In Mr. Trump’s second term, the Justice Department has brought about 200 cases against individuals for voter fraud, far more than the roughly dozen cases that were brought under the Biden Justice Department.

At the same time, the Justice Department has lost dozens of lawsuits it brought against state and local officials over how they have administered elections, including last week in California. In that case, the department requested that California be required to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots that the department claimed were from noncitizens.

The rejection by a grand jury — what is known as a no true bill — was once exceedingly rare. But they have become much more common, especially in Federal District Court in Washington, where Mr. Trump’s political appointees have tried to push through several of his vengeance prosecutions.

Such failures have become common enough that the chief judge in the District of Columbia, James E. Boasberg, has instructed grand jury foremen and forewomen to alert the court if they reject an indictment.

In the past week alone, prosecutors in Washington have faced a series of resounding setbacks.

Last Tuesday, grand jurors rejected an effort by the Justice Department’s civil rights division to charge Ms. Hutchinson with lying during her testimony to the House select committee investigating Mr. Trump’s role in the Jan. 6 riot.

On Monday, a judge dismissed charges against two former F.B.I. officials accused of lying to Congress, delivering an embarrassing defeat to Ms. Pirro’s office.

Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui threw out a criminal complaint used to charge the two former officials — Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides — because prosecutors were unable to persuade him that there was probable cause that the two defendants had actually committed crimes.

In an address from the bench, Judge Faruqui said that he believed prosecutors had charged the former officials by complaint, not by an indictment, because they had a poor record of presenting cases to grand juries.

Judge Faruqui was alerted on Friday to the failure in the voting fraud case — one of several grand jury rejections that he has personally been informed of.

In February, a grand jury declined to indict six Democratic lawmakers who released a video last year reminding military and intelligence personnel of their obligations to disobey illegal orders.

Ms. Pirro’s office has failed to obtain indictments in other cases as well, including several stemming from the president’s use of the military to crack down on local crime.

Aishvarya Kavi contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Delivers a Closing Midterm Message. Mostly About Landscaping.
item.description:
President Trump was standing in front of the Reflecting Pool on Monday afternoon, doing a little reflecting of his own.

“For some reason,” he was saying, the Washington Monument mirrored in the newly reopened pool behind him, “the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms. But we gave this a very strong shot.”

It was the day before the election, and the president had decided to come here, a place that excites him, to talk about many of the topics that make him happiest. Trouble is, almost none of those topics have anything to do with the issues that are driving this election.

At a time when voters have made clear they’re most concerned with the high prices of gas and groceries and a new war in the Middle East, Mr. Trump used his final in-person appearance before Americans head to the polls to talk about drain pipes, top soil, limestone, fountains and his favorite kind of columns.

“The pipes now are totally renovated,” Mr. Trump said. Propped up next to him was a poster board showing an aerial view of the pool, with this caption: “Back, and more beautiful than ever!”

The “brand-new pipes,” Mr. Trump said, are “very important in terms of the algae and other things. And it’s a complete job, and we’re very proud of it.”

The Lincoln Memorial in front of him, Mr. Trump addressed a small audience seated in folding chairs. There were a few dozen National Park Service employees, reporters, White House officials and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. At one point early in his speech, Mr. Trump beckoned to a young man who bounded up onstage with a stack of large printouts under his arm.

“Great,” Mr. Trump said as he took the stack and began rifling through it. He held up one of the printouts. It was a photograph of what looked like a rusty drainpipe. Another photograph showed a dumpster filled with detritus.

“This is another example of what it looked like just at water level and below,” he explained as he waved another photograph aloft. Every so often, he would look over his shoulder to check on the body of water behind him. “It’s a massive piece of pool,” he said, sounding impressed. It looked clean, dark and choppy on this early November day.

After he finished with the pictures, the president turned to other matters of national interest. Matters including: the nature of Corinthian columns (“the most beautiful in the world”); the soul of grass generally, and Bermuda grass specifically (“like the human being, grass has a life also”); the endurance of granite (“it literally has thousands of years of life”); the renovation of a public golf course on the Potomac that he’s planning; statues; the White House ballroom; graffiti; and the new White House helipad.

“The helipad,” Mr. Trump said, “was desperately needed.”

In the history of American politics, the speech may go down as one of the more unusual closing messages on the eve of an election. But it was a pretty good crystallization of what matters to Mr. Trump as he heads into the lame duck phase of his second term — despite, or maybe because of, his depressed poll numbers and voter unhappiness over the economy, corruption and an unresolved war.

And now here he was, using his final in-person address before the election to talk more about his chryselephantine fantasies of ballrooms and arches and Corinthian columns.

“The president’s a builder,” Mr. Burgum said from the little stage on Monday. “You can’t keep him away!” Large signs that aides had duct-taped to the stage before the president’s arrival read: “RESTORING OUR CAPITAL.”

He made some of his usual comments about the war with Iran, the U.S. economy and various culture war issues, but he did not even attempt to explain how any of the renovation projects that were the focus of the speech related to any of the issues animating the midterm elections.

“I’ve traveled all across the country, spoken at all of these rallies I’ve done over the last two and a half weeks,” he said. “America is ready to go. They’re ready to vote. I hope they’re ready to do the right thing.”

It seemed almost as though he had run out of things to say about politics and governance, and like he simply wanted to talk about what sparks joy for him.

“We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation,” Mr. Trump said, “but for that you don’t have enough time.”
